evidence.raw_text: Let's Get Visual -Testing Visual Analogies and Metaphors for Conveying Privacy Policies and Data Handling Information

With EU-GDPR and related regulations, the responsibility to make privacy-related decisions such as to provide informed consent to data handling practices mainly rests with the user. However, current lengthy privacy policies and often deceptive cookie notices rarely facilitate truly informed consent. Related work on privacy icons or structuring privacy policies aims to enhance users' understanding but achieve mixed results. In a between-subjects study with N=379 participants we thus explored the potential of embedding privacy information in visual metaphors and analogies to support informed decision-making. Additionally, we explored whether dynamic feedback helped users understand the implications of their decisions. While both visual and textual information and feedback appeared to support users' understanding of data handling practices and alignment with personal preferences, with no significant differences between conditions, users perceived visualizations as more suitable and aesthetically pleasing than text. This indicates potential for using visual contexts to enhance informed consent not only within existing cookie notices but also in emerging tools such as privacy assistants or related privacy-enhancing technologies. Future work should investigate differences to currently deployed solutions and the effect of perceived pleasantness of design variants on users' understanding and decisions. 2303 2025 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)

Introduction Access to personal information is a sensitive issue as it can be misused for various purposes not intended by the person. While the collection, processing, or tracking of personal information may be essential for the functioning of some online services, there is a huge potential for service providers to make use of personal data beyond this, for example for marketing purposes. To avoid unintended use of personal data, current regu- lations such as the European General Data Privacy Regula- tion (EU-GDPR) first of all suggest scarce data collection. Second, regulations suggest that users have to provide their informed consent for data collection purposes that exceed the essential functioning of the service to provide users with control over their personal data and privacy. On websites this regulation often becomes visible in the form of privacy poli- cies or cookie consent notices that ask for the users' consent to data collection purposes such as increased functionality, statistical analysis, or marketing purposes. However, despite these efforts, information on what kind of personal data service providers collect and how they handle it is often lengthy, complicated, and difficult to understand for users. Research shows that privacy policies are thus seldom read [1]. While cookie consent notices already aim to cluster online-tracking information with regards to the purpose of information collection and handling, the consent notices are often inscrutable and the cookie categories unclear for the user [2]. Furthermore, the collection purposes such as “Strictly Necessary” or “Marketing” do not contain the information users wish to know about how their data is handled [3] thus casting doubt on their capability to actually inform users. In addition, the frequent use of deceptive patterns may lure users to consent to all cookies even if this is not in the user's interest [4], [5]. Thus, an informed consent as intended by EU-GDPR is often questionable. To address this challenge, one line of research focused on structuring and shortening privacy policies to make the relevant information more easily detectable. Yet, Angulo et al. [6] found that textual information is not sufficient in conveying privacy information and instead suggest the in- clusion of visualizations, such as suitable icons or symbols. A second line of research focused on facilitating decision- making through providing users with a privacy rating or label. This often already includes some kind of evaluation such as a privacy score. Also, in line with the suggestion by Angulo et al. [6] many of these ratings have been in a visual form to allow for a quick understanding and interpretation of the score. Another line of research focused on the development of icon sets to convey the data handling practices to users in a visual way, such as the Privacy Icons Forum [7] that lists a number of current projects and global initiatives. However, unlike standardized icon sets in other areas, e.g., traffic signs or warning signs in the chemical industry, there is no single standard set that everyone learns and knows as of yet. Even recent and promising attempts evaluated by Habib et al. [8] come to the conclusion that 2303 DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00240 icons still have to be accompanied by textual information to avoid ambiguity in the interpretation. Thus, while all these research lines are highly relevant, supporting users in making informed privacy choices is still an open research challenge. Therefore, this research aims to enhance knowledge transfer to provide substance for informed decision making. Building on related work and insights from current projects and initiatives, we aim to support users' privacy choices by visualizing privacy information in a graphical context that includes but is not limited to icons. To foster understanding of online data handling practices as described, e.g., in privacy policies and cookie notices, we aim to make use of visual metaphors and analogies to provide a meaningful context for privacy icons and to thereby support a quick overview and understanding. Several studies showed that users can better learn from a combination of text and visualizations as compared to just text [9], [10], [11], [12], [13]. Visuals were found to be useful as they improve comprehension [14], [15], [16], [17], [18], [19], [20], [21], minimize redundancy and ambiguity [16], [19], as well as encourage development of mental models [22], [23]. As several studies have already found positive effects of using visual analogies in science education [24], we were interested in trying to leverage these positive effects also for privacy education purposes. The aim of this research is to graphically convey what kind of data is collected, processed and shared for what purpose. In line with the EU-GDPR requirement for informed consent rather than suggesting a certain choice - neither privacy- preserving nor privacy-invasive - the graphical depictions do not include privacy ratings or recommendations but present the information in a neutral way. Our research is guided by the following overarching research question (RQ): How can meaningful visualizations that provide a context for privacy icons and textual infor- mation be designed to support users' informed consent with regards to privacy choices? With regards to the intended knowledge transfer for informed decision making, we aim to answer the following sub-questions: • RQ1: Do users understand the selected data han- dling option and its implications for privacy-related data processing? • RQ2: Is the users' selection in line with their privacy preferences? • RQ3: How do users evaluate the contextual privacy visualizations in comparison to textual approaches? • RQ4: Does dynamic and situation-specific privacy feedback support users in understanding the conse- quences of their privacy choices? To answer these research questions, we have first searched related work for already existing and evaluated vi- sualizations, as well as developed our own visualizations that make use of visual metaphors and analogies. Afterwards, we conducted three pilot studies and a workshop to iteratively select and improve the visualizations. Then, we set out to evaluate the six selected visualizations in comparison to two control conditions in a between-subject online study with 379 participants that interacted with a fictional web shop to explore user understanding, interaction, perception, and acceptance. Additionally, we tested whether dynamic and situation-specific feedback on the privacy implications resulting from the selection of data handling purposes, i.e., how a specific personal information would be used or shared with third parties, helped users to better understand the consequences of their choices. The results revealed that while visual as compared to textual depiction of data handling practices did not impact on the users' data handling purpose selection or under- standing differently, our visual approach to showcasing the privacy implications of data handling purposes seemed to support users in making informed decisions as compared to currently wide-spread privacy policies or cookie notices. As such, users overall expressed a high level of understanding and alignment of their selection with their privacy prefer- ences. Furthermore, our self-developed visualizations were perceived as more aesthetic and suitable to illustrate data handling practices as compared to text and appeared to catch the users' attention as indicated by high recall rates. Dy- namic feedback on privacy implications was rated positively indicating potential to enhance user understanding. The contribution of this research is three-fold: First, this research bridges a gap between existing promising approaches to facilitate or visualize privacy- related information and the knowledge-transfer required for informed consent by providing visual privacy information in a meaningful visual context. Second, the findings provide valuable insights into how information can be structured to quickly inform users about the implications of different data handling purposes to foster truly informed decision making as envisioned by the EU- GDPR. For example, the results demonstrate the suitability of the approach to support users in making decisions in line with their preferences. Third, the evaluated approach not only provides insights for structuring or visualizing existing privacy policies or enhancing understandability of cookie choices but could also inform the design of current privacy enhancing approaches such as privacy assistants in which users define their privacy preferences to be implemented across websites and services. 2. Related Work We summarize prior research on informed consent and privacy decision support relevant to our study. 2.1. Facilitating privacy policies Our approach differs from that line of research in that we focus on visual rather than textual information provision. Condensing privacy policies can reduce reading times but may hinder comprehension [25]. Prior work explored struc- turing policies [26], automating annotations [27], translating source code [28], and extracting data [29]. 2304
